1.title: See: Look at the Colour — Systematic Appearance Analysis
1.html:
Tilt the glass at about 45 degrees against a white background (such as a tabletop or white paper), and observe from the centre of the wine (core) out to the edge where it meets the glass (rim), analysing three dimensions in turn:

  • Clarity: clear and bright, or cloudy — cloudiness is usually a warning sign of a winemaking fault
  • Intensity: pale, medium or deep — observe how much the colour graduates towards the rim
  • Colour: Alsace whites typically range from pale lemon-green (young Riesling) to golden with copper tones (mature Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris)

⚠️ An important mindset: the depth of a wine's colour has no direct relationship with its quality — colour is only one clue to variety, ripeness and ageing potential.
2.title: Sniff: Smell the Aroma — Awakening the Memory Bank of Smell
2.html:
First swirl the wine gently so it contacts the air fully and releases its aroma molecules; then bring the rim of the glass to your nose, take a deep breath in through the nose and exhale gently through the mouth, repeating once or twice to capture the full aroma profile. Analyse three dimensions systematically:

  • Condition: confirm the wine is free of faults (such as cork taint or oxidation off-odours)
  • Development: youthful (primary fruit dominant), developing, or fully developed (tertiary ageing aromas dominant)
  • Intensity & Aroma Characteristics: how strong the fruit is and the specific aroma types — Riesling often shows lime, honey and slate minerality; Gewurztraminer intense lychee and rose; Pinot Gris delicate floral notes with lemon and citrus
3.title: Sip: Taste the Flavour — Taking Apart the Seven Structural Dimensions
3.html:
Hold a small amount of wine in the mouth for a few seconds and chew it gently, drawing in a little air with the lips to amplify flavour perception, then exhale through the nose to feel the retronasal aroma, and finally choose to swallow or spit. Take apart the following dimensions systematically:

DimensionTypical Expression of Alsace Whites
SweetnessDry is the mainstream, with faint residual sugar common in Pinot Gris / Gewurztraminer
AcidityHigh in Riesling; medium to lowish in Gewurztraminer / Pinot Gris
BodyLight in Sylvaner / Pinot Blanc; full and rich in Gewurztraminer / Pinot Gris
Flavour Intensity (Fruit Intensity)Varies by variety and appellation tier (Grand Cru is usually more concentrated)
AlcoholUsually 12.5–14%, higher in VT / SGN
Finish (Length)The finish of Grand Cru and noble-rot sweet wines is usually long

💡 Sparkling wine (Crémant d'Alsace) is additionally assessed for the delicacy and persistence of the bubbles — these two are key clues to the quality of traditional-method craft.
4.question: In systematic tasting, what is the most important mindset when observing a wine's colour?
4.options.0: The deeper the colour, the better the quality
4.options.1: The depth of a wine's colour has no direct relationship with its quality; it is only one clue to variety, ripeness and ageing potential
4.options.2: The paler the colour, the better the quality
4.options.3: Colour has nothing to do with quality and need not be observed
4.explanation: One important mindset in systematic tasting: the depth of a wine's colour has no direct relationship with its quality — colour is only a clue to help judge variety character, ripeness and stage of ageing, and quality cannot be judged from colour depth alone, which is the most common tasting mistake for beginners.
5.message: Tasting with the WSET SAT framework complete!
5.keyPoints.0: See: observe Clarity, Intensity and Colour at a 45-degree angle — colour depth is unrelated to quality
5.keyPoints.2: Sip: the seven structural dimensions — sweetness, acidity, body, flavour intensity, alcohol, finish, with sparkling wine also assessed for bubble delicacy and persistence
5.keyPoints.3: Systematic tasting turns subjective "tastes good / doesn't taste good" into an objective language that can be communicated and compared
